title: VANKO-ABDUCTED-ZEBRAFISH: Anatomy of an Insider Trade-Secret Theft
subtitle: How a trusted StarkResearch employee collected, staged, disguised, and cloud-exfiltrated classified IP using only his own credentials and signed tools — and why his cleanup failed.
intro_line: This is not a malware case: every step rides on valid access and legitimate, signed software — which is exactly what makes the cross-source forensic timeline so damning.
kill_chain_summary: 1. Collect: Anthony Vanko uses his own credentials and authorized share access to copy the classified Level_* corpus off \\STARK-FILESERVE into OneDrive (file-COPY signature, 2016-04-30 18:10).
2. Stage the mule: he interactively creates a masquerade local account, "defaultprinter," to segregate the loot from his own profile (2016-06-18 20:40:54).
3. Stage the loot: a 2.6 MB classified archive (temp.zip) lands on the defaultprinter Desktop, then is deleted the same evening (22:22:09).
4. Realize scope: a Level-12 "Project Nehemiah" document is actively opened (Word owner-lock recovered), pushing realized exposure above the assumed Level 5-8 tier.
5. Coordinate: he replies to the foreign-recruiter channel (Merrick -> handler Bulgakov), "RE: Potential Opportunity?", with three attachments (2016-06-27 21:22:49).
6. Disguise: the corpus is archived with signed 7-Zip as "vacation photos.7z" (2016-06-30 01:28).
7. Exfiltrate: the disguised archive is uploaded to Dropbox account 984347879 (01:46:06), with SRUM corroborating dual Dropbox+OneDrive egress.
8. Cover tracks: SDelete wipes the originals, the prefetch and 1.9 GB Dropbox folder are purged — but Volume Shadow Copies preserve all of it.

scenes.title: Insider Collected the Classified Corpus from the StarkResearch File Server
scenes.mitre: T1078 (Valid Accounts) + T1039 (Data from Network Shared Drive)
scenes.key_fact: Operating with his own valid credentials, Anthony Vanko used native file-sharing access to the StarkResearch server (\\STARK-FILESERVE, \\192.168.1.5, \\192.168.1.3) and copied the classified document corpus down into C:\Users\PC User\OneDrive\Documents\Level_* on 2016-04-30 18:10 UTC. The copy is proven by MFT $SI timestamps showing 2016-04-30 creation against preserved 2015-2016 authoring (modified) dates — a file-COPY signature, not timestamp manipulation.

artifacts.source: NTUSER.DAT registry hive (RECmd) — provenance / the file-server access history
artifacts.locator: C:\Users\PC User\NTUSER.DAT — TypedPaths url7-url10: \\192.168.1.5, \\STARK-FILESERVE, \\192.168.1.3, Network
artifacts.shows: The PC User account typed UNC paths directly to the StarkResearch file server, establishing it as the source of the stolen IP (VANKO-P3-005).

artifacts.source: $MFT master file table ($SI, MFTECmd, step_021) — the copy event landing on disk
artifacts.locator: $MFT $SI: Created = 2016-04-30 18:10 with $SI Modified = original authoring dates, e.g. Stark_Level_12_Wolverine_Dossier modified 2015-03-21; Stark_TS-Level8A_CryoDNA modified 2015-12-22; STARK-TS-Level7-CryoDNA modified 2016-03-15 — under C:\Users\PC User\OneDrive\Documents\Level_*
artifacts.shows: Created-after-modified ordering is a textbook file-COPY signature: $SI Created = the 2016-04-30 copy-to-OneDrive time, $SI Modified = the original StarkResearch authoring date.

artifacts.source: VSS Store2 differential (libvshadow, vss2_fls.txt) — corroborating that a Level_* corpus existed and was actively used
artifacts.locator: C:\Users\PC User\OneDrive\Documents\Level_12\~$...Project_Nehemiah 4.docx (Word owner-lock recovered from the 2016-11-04 shadow copy)
artifacts.shows: A Level-12 document under the same OneDrive\Documents\Level_* tree was actively opened, confirming the copied corpus was real classified material (VANKO-P4-004).

scenes.correlation: The two primary artifacts come from independent sources and converge on the same conclusion. The NTUSER TypedPaths (registry) prove WHERE the data came from — the operator manually navigated to \\STARK-FILESERVE / \\192.168.1.5 / \\192.168.1.3. The $MFT $SI timestamps (filesystem) prove the RESULT — those server files landing under OneDrive\\Documents\\Level_* with a created time (2016-04-30 18:10) that is LATER than their modified/authoring time (2015-2016). That created>modified ordering is the deterministic fingerprint of a file copy: a copy operation resets the destination's creation time to the moment of copy while carrying the original document's authoring (modified) time forward. The registry says he reached the server; the MFT says server documents arrived locally by copy; and the VSS-recovered Level_12 Word lock confirms the same Level_* tree held genuine classified material that was opened. Three sources, one event chain.
scenes.what_it_means: This is the Collection stage of the insider theft and the origin of the entire case: the classified zebrafish-DNA, cell-regeneration, CryoDNA and Ion-Thruster corpus did not come from an external breach — a trusted employee used his own legitimate credentials and authorized network-share access to pull it off the StarkResearch server onto his workstation, where it was later staged, archived as 'vacation photos.7z', and exfiltrated. Crucially, the timestamp anomaly here is NOT timestomping (that hypothesis was tested and refuted, VANKO-P1-003); it is honest copy provenance, which makes it stronger evidence — it ties specific classified server documents to a specific copy event on a specific date by a specific account.

scenes.title: Masquerade local account "defaultprinter" created by PC User as a staging mule (T1136.001)
scenes.mitre: T1136.001 (Create Account: Local Account); enables T1074.001 (Local Data Staging)
scenes.key_fact: On 2016-06-18 20:40:54 UTC the insider principal PC User interactively created a non-default local account named "defaultprinter" on STARKSURFACE (Security.evtx EventID 4720 record_id 19669, with the 4724 password-set in the same second, SubjectUserName=PC User / TargetUserName=defaultprinter). The account was not a Windows-default principal but a masquerade staging mule: its newly-provisioned profile directory carried a 2.6 MB classified archive (temp.zip) on its Desktop.

artifacts.source: Windows Security event log (EvtxECmd over Security.evtx)
artifacts.locator: /Windows/System32/winevt/Logs/Security.evtx — EventID 4720 record_id 19669 @2016-06-18T20:40:54Z (+ EventID 4724 record_id 19672, same second); SubjectUserName=PC User, TargetUserName=defaultprinter, Computer=StarkSurface
artifacts.shows: The account-create + password-set pair proving PC User interactively built the defaultprinter account at the start of the exfil window.

artifacts.locator: SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\ProfileList — profile path C:\Users\defaultprinter
artifacts.shows: A real on-disk user profile was materialized for defaultprinter, corroborating the event-log creation in an independent artifact class (registry, not the log).

artifacts.source: Recycle Bin $I metadata + carved $R content (TSK / MFTECmd)
artifacts.locator: /$Recycle.Bin $I record → C:\Users\defaultprinter\Desktop\temp.zip, 2,603,690 B, deleted 2016-06-18 22:22:09 UTC; recovered as $RZQSNFO.zip
artifacts.shows: The defaultprinter Desktop held a 2.6 MB classified staging archive (Ion Thruster / ZF-DNA / cell-regen), proving the account was used as a staging mule rather than a benign system principal.

scenes.correlation: Three independent artifact classes converge on one account. The Security.evtx 4720/4724 pair fixes the creation act and the acting principal (SubjectUser=PC User), and the 4724 password-set firing in the same second as the 4720 is the signature of an interactive, fully-provisioned account creation rather than a transient system stub. The SOFTWARE-hive ProfileList entry independently confirms the OS actually built and persisted a C:\Users\defaultprinter profile — an event-log claim cross-checked against a registry artifact written by a different subsystem. The Recycle Bin $I record then shows that this profile's Desktop carried a 2,603,690-byte classified archive deleted 1h 41m after creation (20:40:54 -> 22:22:09 same day) — the tight intra-window timeline plus the classified contents (recovered by carving $RZQSNFO.zip) establish use and intent. "defaultprinter" is not a Windows-default principal, so its existence, its provisioned profile, and its classified Desktop payload only cohere under the staging-mule interpretation; this cross-source agreement is what promoted finding VANKO-P1-001 from candidate to confirmed.
scenes.what_it_means: The insider deliberately created a throwaway local account with an innocuous, system-sounding name ("defaultprinter") to segregate and stage the stolen classified material away from his own PC User profile — a defense-evasion / blame-deflection move, not legitimate administration. Because the account creation is captured in the audit log, corroborated by the registry-persisted profile, and tied to a recovered 2.6 MB classified archive on that profile's Desktop, the staging step is established by independent evidence rather than inference. It is the pivot between collecting the corpus from the file server and the later archive/disguise/cloud-exfil steps, and it attributes that staging directly to PC User (Anthony Vanko).

scenes.title: Classified 2.6 MB temp.zip staged on the masquerade account's Desktop
scenes.mitre: T1074.001 (with T1136.001 account creation, T1070.004 anti-forensic wipe)
scenes.key_fact: A 2,603,690-byte archive `temp.zip` was staged on the Desktop of the non-default local account `defaultprinter` — created interactively by `PC User` 1h41m earlier — then deleted to the Recycle Bin at 2016-06-18 22:22:09 UTC and recovered by carving as `$RZQSNFO.zip`, whose contents are Ion-Thruster weaponization material, zebrafish-DNA splice notes, and cell-regeneration research (VANKO-P2-001 / T1074.001).

artifacts.source: Windows Security event log (EvtxECmd over Security.evtx)
artifacts.locator: /Windows/System32/winevt/Logs/Security.evtx — EventID 4720 record_id 19669 @2016-06-18T20:40:54Z (4724 record_id 19672, same second); SubjectUserName=PC User, TargetUserName=defaultprinter
artifacts.shows: PC User interactively created the masquerade local account defaultprinter at 20:40:54 UTC, establishing the staging container before any file was placed in it.

artifacts.locator: /$Recycle.Bin $I record: C:\Users\defaultprinter\Desktop\temp.zip — 2,603,690 B, deleted 2016-06-18 22:22:09 UTC; recovered $R record carved as $RZQSNFO.zip (collected/deleted-recycle/)
artifacts.shows: The 2.6 MB archive lived on the masquerade account's Desktop and was deleted 1h41m after the account was created; the carved $R copy yields Ion-Thruster / ZF-DNA / cell-regen content.

artifacts.locator: vss2_fls.txt deleted(*) entry: Users/defaultprinter/Desktop/temp.zip (0 bytes), with temp.zip~RF9b00d6e.TMP remnant
artifacts.shows: The same Desktop path survives in the 2016-11-04 shadow copy at 0 bytes, evidencing the later SDelete secure-wipe and confirming the archive's path/identity across two independent stores.

scenes.correlation: Three independent artifact classes converge on one path, C:\Users\defaultprinter\Desktop\temp.zip. The Security event log fixes the account's birth (4720/4724 at 20:40:54), and the Recycle Bin $I record fixes the archive's deletion (22:22:09) — a tight 1h41m staging-then-delete sequence on a principal that did not exist that morning. The $I-recorded logical size (2,603,690 B) ties the deleted-object metadata to the carved $R content ($RZQSNFO.zip), so the byte count, the path, and the recovered classified payload all describe the same file. The libvshadow VSS differential independently reproduces the exact same path at 0 bytes, corroborating both the location (cross-store agreement: $I metadata + shadow-copy directory entry) and the subsequent anti-forensic wipe. The conclusion holds because no single source carries it: event log = who/when created, $I = what/size/when deleted, carving = classified content, VSS = independent path confirmation plus the wipe signature.
scenes.what_it_means: This is the concrete act of insider data staging. The subject did not stash the stolen material under his own profile; he spun up a throw-away local account that masquerades as a benign system principal ("defaultprinter") and used its Desktop as a holding pen for a 2.6 MB archive of the most sensitive material in the case — Ion-Thruster weaponization, zebrafish-DNA splice notes, and cell-regeneration research. The deliberate sequence (create account → stage classified archive → delete) and the later secure-wipe show intent and consciousness of guilt, not routine work. The anti-forensic deletion failed because Volume Shadow Copies preserved the path; the staged archive is therefore documented end-to-end rather than lost.

scenes.title: Realized scope breach: Level-12 "Project Nehemiah" document was actively opened (T1530)
scenes.mitre: T1530 (Data from Cloud Storage); corpus provenance T1039; recovery via T1070.004-defeated anti-forensics
scenes.key_fact: Volume Shadow Copy recovery proves the subject opened a classified Level-12 document — Microsoft Word created a `~$` owner-lock file for `Stark TS-Level 12_Project_Nehemiah 4.docx` inside the OneDrive `Level_12` folder, and Word only writes that hidden lock when a document is actively opened by a user. This places realized exposure at Level-12, beyond the original Level 5-8 brief, even though the classified corpus itself was provenance-proven by copy-signatures (not content-scan, which OOXML compression defeats).

artifacts.locator: C:\Users\PC User\OneDrive\Documents\Level_12\~$Stark TS-Level 12_Project_Nehemiah 4.docx
artifacts.shows: Word owner-lock (~$) file recovered from the shadow copy — its existence is created only when the document is opened, proving an active open of a Level-12 file.

artifacts.source: libvshadow VSS differential file listing (vss2_fls.txt, Store2)
artifacts.locator: vss2_fls.txt — deleted(*) entries incl. Users/PC User/OneDrive/Documents/Level_12/~$...Project_Nehemiah 4.docx (1 of 23,848 deleted-at-snapshot entries)
artifacts.shows: The lock file was deleted on the live volume but preserved in the 2016-10-14/2016-11-04 shadow copies — recovered alongside the SDelete prefetch and 0-byte temp.zip, anchoring it to the same anti-forensic cleanup.

artifacts.locator: Stark_Level_12_Wolverine_Dossier — $SI Created 2016-04-30 18:10 vs $SI Modified 2015-03-21
artifacts.shows: Level-12 material existed in the OneDrive corpus via a file-COPY signature (created-after-modified) from the StarkResearch server, independently establishing Level-12 content was present to be opened.

scenes.correlation: The conclusion holds on cross-source agreement plus Word's own file-locking semantics. Microsoft Word writes a hidden `~$<name>.docx` owner-lock the instant a user opens a document and removes it on close; recovering that lock file for "Project_Nehemiah 4.docx" is therefore positive evidence of an active open, not mere presence on disk. The lock surfaces only because libvshadow's differential of the 2016-11-04 Store2 snapshot preserved it after deletion — and it appears in the same 23,848-entry deleted-at-snapshot set as the SDelete prefetch (SDELETE.EXE-FBA93810.pf) and the 0-byte wiped temp.zip, tying the Level-12 access to the same post-exfil cleanup window the rest of the chain documents. Independently, the $MFT copy-signature ($SI Created 2016-04-30 18:10 against a preserved 2015 authoring date) confirms Level-12 documents were copied from the StarkResearch file server into the OneDrive\Documents\Level_12 path in the first place, so the open was of genuinely classified Level-12 material. Two independent artifact stores (VSS file system + MFT) and one structural fact (Word lock semantics) converge.
scenes.what_it_means: The breach exceeded its assumed limits. The original brief scoped exposure to Level 5-8 trade secrets, but the recovered Word owner-lock proves the subject actively opened a Level-12 document, "Project Nehemiah" — a higher classification band. For damage assessment and prosecution this raises the realized exposure ceiling and shows the insider reached into material above his presumed access tier. Stated honestly: the lock proves the document was OPENED; it does not by itself prove that this specific file was among the three undisclosed email attachments or the Dropbox payload (attachment content was never extracted), and the classified content was verified by copy-provenance rather than by reading the documents. The Level-12 open is nonetheless a confirmed, examiner-approved finding (VANKO-P4-004).

scenes.title: Foreign-Handler Coordination: Two-Way Reply Carrying Three Attachments
scenes.key_fact: Mailbox analysis of the subject's Gmail OST confirms an outbound reply "RE: Potential Opportunity?" sent by Anthony Vanko at 2016-06-27 21:22:49 UTC to mmerr001@gmail.com (Michael Merrick, the recruiter introducing Russian handler Vladimir Bulgakov), carrying three attachments (n_attachments=3) in direct reply to Merrick's inbound recruitment message received 3h58m earlier. This establishes two-way contact with the foreign handler channel; the attachment content was not extracted, so classified-exfiltration-by-email is NOT asserted — only the coordination is confirmed.

artifacts.locator: /Users/PC User/AppData/Local/Microsoft/Outlook/anthony.vanko@gmail.com (1).ost — message from Anthony Vanko, subject "RE: Potential Opportunity?", 2016-06-27 21:22:49, n_attachments=3, to mmerr001@gmail.com
artifacts.shows: The actual outbound reply: sender, subject, exact UTC timestamp, recipient, and the count of three attachments.

artifacts.source: Gmail OST message store (inbound recruitment, same store)
artifacts.locator: /Users/PC User/AppData/Local/Microsoft/Outlook/anthony.vanko@gmail.com (1).ost — inbound message from mmerr001@gmail.com (Michael Merrick), subject "Potential Opportunity?", 2016-06-27 17:24, introducing Vladimir Bulgakov
artifacts.shows: The originating recruitment email the reply answers — same thread, same recipient, naming handler Bulgakov, time-ordered before the reply.

artifacts.source: SRUM network-transfer accounting (cross-source corroboration of exfil intent in-window)
artifacts.locator: /Windows/System32/sru/SRUDB.dat (SrumECmd) — Dropbox Client+Update bytes_sent 2.6MB+837KB; OneDrive bytes_sent, corroborating Dropbox account 984347879 upload @2016-06-30 01:46:06
artifacts.shows: Independent network artifact placing active cloud exfil egress in the same June-2016 window, corroborating exfiltration intent that frames the handler coordination.

scenes.correlation: The two OST records form a matched request/response pair within one message store: Merrick's inbound "Potential Opportunity?" lands at 17:24 and the subject's outbound "RE: Potential Opportunity?" departs at 21:22:49 the same day — the RE: subject prefix, identical counterparty (mmerr001@gmail.com), and 3h58m forward time-ordering are the technical signature of a genuine two-way reply rather than an isolated or spoofed message. Both messages are parsed from the same forensically-recovered OST (1,592 messages), so sender/recipient/timestamp/attachment-count are read directly from the store, not inferred. The SRUM SRUDB.dat egress (a different artifact class — network accounting, not mailbox) independently shows active cloud exfiltration days later in the same window, providing cross-source agreement that the coordination sits inside a live exfiltration operation. Crucially, no artifact asserts the three attachments contained classified material: carve_pst_iocs parsed headers only, so the corroboration proves coordination and intent context, not email-borne classified transfer.
scenes.what_it_means: The subject did not merely receive a recruitment overture — he actively answered it, replying to the foreign recruiter channel (Merrick → handler Bulgakov) within hours and attaching three files. This is affirmative, two-way coordination with a foreign handler during the exfiltration window, materially distinguishing an insider who engaged a hostile buyer/recruiter from one who was merely solicited. The honest limit is stated plainly for the jury: because the attachments were never extracted or hashed, the case does NOT claim the three files were the stolen trade secrets; the email channel evidences handler coordination (T1567), while the proven classified exfiltration runs through the separately-evidenced Dropbox/OneDrive cloud path (T1567.002).

scenes.title: Classified payload disguised as "vacation photos.7z" via signed tools weaponized in sequence
scenes.mitre: T1560.001 (Archive Collected Data: Archive via Utility) + T1036 (Masquerading); chained with T1070.004 (Indicator Removal: File Deletion)
scenes.key_fact: The stolen classified corpus was archived with legitimate signed 7-Zip and disguised as a holiday-photo container, "vacation photos.7z" (SHA-256 b210bcd89fbde5d3b0816e1834483f7b82adf8565fd880d49930c25450ca7e31), created 2016-06-30 01:28 UTC. No custom malware was used; the probative element is the executed sequence of signed utilities within the exfil window — 7-Zip archive (06-29 20:26) -> SDelete 10x secure-wipe of the originals (06-30 01:30:52) -> Dropbox upload (06-30 01:46:06).

artifacts.locator: C:\Users\PC User\Downloads\vacation photos.7z  —  created 2016-06-30 01:28 UTC; SHA-256 b210bcd89fbde5d3b0816e1834483f7b82adf8565fd880d49930c25450ca7e31
artifacts.shows: The disguised payload itself: classified docs archived under an innocuous holiday-photo filename (the masquerade), with its content hash and creation time fixed by the MFT.

artifacts.locator: C:\Windows\Prefetch  —  7ZG.EXE x9, 7ZFM.EXE x3 (last exec 2016-06-29 20:26); Amcache.hve  7z1602-x64.exe SHA1 prefix 0d2c251d
artifacts.shows: The signed 7-Zip archiver (Igor Pavlov) actually executed on the host immediately before the .7z was created, attributing the archive to a real tool run rather than a phantom file.

artifacts.locator: C:\Windows\Prefetch  —  SDELETE.EXE x10 (last exec 2016-06-30 01:30:52); Amcache.hve  sdelete.exe SHA1 prefix ab48396a
artifacts.shows: SysInternals SDelete (signed) ran 10 times, last firing ~2 minutes after the .7z was created, secure-wiping the original staged files — the anti-forensic step in the chain.

scenes.correlation: The three artifacts come from independent stores (file-system $MFT/LNK, execution Prefetch, and the Amcache registry hive) yet interlock on a single tight timeline. The 7-Zip archiver's last run (Prefetch 06-29 20:26) precedes the creation of vacation photos.7z ($MFT 06-30 01:28), which precedes SDelete's last run (Prefetch 06-30 01:30:52) by about two minutes, which precedes the Dropbox upload of that same .7z (aggregation.dbx / SRUM, 06-30 01:46:06). Amcache independently pins each tool to a specific signed binary by SHA1 (7z1602-x64.exe 0d2c251d; sdelete.exe ab48396a), so the execution evidence is not merely a name match. No single binary is incriminating in isolation — each is a benign, signed utility — but archive-then-wipe-then-upload in this order, within this ~18-minute window, is data-theft and anti-forensic tradecraft, not routine administration. The masquerade conclusion (T1036) rests on the mismatch between the "vacation photos" filename and the corroborated classified provenance of the staged material (MFT copy-signatures from \\STARK-FILESERVE), while T1560.001 rests on the proven 7-Zip execution producing the container.
scenes.what_it_means: This is the moment the stolen trade secrets were packaged for exit and the actor tried to cover his tracks. An insider with valid access used only legitimate, signed software to bundle classified zebrafish-DNA and cell-regeneration material into a file deliberately named to look like personal vacation photos, then immediately secure-wiped the originals before uploading the disguised archive to Dropbox. Because the activity rode entirely on trusted tools, it evaded malware detection — yet the cross-source timeline (file creation, tool execution, and binary hashes) reconstructs the intent unambiguously. The secure-deletion did not succeed: Volume Shadow Copies (2016-10-14 / 2016-11-04) later preserved the wiped artifacts and the deleted SDelete prefetch, so the cleanup itself became evidence of consciousness of guilt.

scenes.title: Dual Cloud Exfil: Dropbox Upload Plus OneDrive (SRUM-Corroborated)
scenes.mitre: T1567.002 (Exfiltration to Cloud Storage); related T1567
scenes.key_fact: The disguised archive vacation photos.7z (SHA-256 b210bcd89fbde5d3b0816e1834483f7b82adf8565fd880d49930c25450ca7e31) was uploaded to Dropbox account 984347879 at 2016-06-30 01:46:06 UTC, recorded in the Dropbox aggregation.dbx client database. Independent SRUM network accounting (SRUDB.dat) confirms both cloud channels actively transmitting: the Dropbox Client and Dropbox Update apps sent 2.6 MB + 837 KB and the Microsoft/OneDrive app sent 8.7 MB — establishing dual cloud egress (T1567.002), not a single channel.

artifacts.locator: /Users/PC User/AppData/Local/Dropbox/aggregation.dbx — record 984347879:/vacation photos.7z, upload 2016-06-30 01:46:06 UTC
artifacts.shows: The Dropbox app's own catalog records the disguised payload being uploaded to a named external account at an exact timestamp.

artifacts.locator: /Windows/System32/sru/SRUDB.dat — Dropbox Client + Dropbox Update BytesSent 2.6 MB + 837 KB; Microsoft/OneDrive BytesSent 8.7 MB / BytesRecv 551 MB
artifacts.shows: OS-level per-application byte accounting independently confirms BOTH Dropbox and OneDrive transmitted data outbound (sent bytes), corroborating two live exfil channels.

artifacts.source: Carved payload hash + OneDrive account identifier
artifacts.locator: vacation photos.7z SHA-256 b210bcd89fbde5d3b0816e1834483f7b82adf8565fd880d49930c25450ca7e31 (foremost/bulk_extractor, $MFT/LNK); OneDrive CID CBDFA76592A9F765 (registry step_018), endpoint storage.live.com
artifacts.shows: The cryptographic hash binds the uploaded Dropbox object to the recovered disguised archive, and the OneDrive CID/endpoint attributes the second channel to the subject's cloud account.

scenes.correlation: Two independent artifact sources of different provenance agree on the same event. The Dropbox-authored aggregation.dbx database places vacation photos.7z into external account 984347879 at 2016-06-30 01:46:06; the Windows-authored SRUM database (SRUDB.dat) — which the subject did not control and did not wipe — shows the Dropbox client/updater applications sending bytes (2.6 MB + 837 KB) in the same window, with the 2.6 MB Dropbox-Client sent total matching the magnitude of the staged archive. A third leg closes the chain: the SHA-256 of the carved on-disk payload (b210bcd8…) matches the object named in the Dropbox upload record, so the file that was uploaded is provably the disguised classified archive. SRUM simultaneously records the Microsoft/OneDrive application transmitting 8.7 MB sent (OneDrive CID CBDFA76592A9F765, endpoint storage.live.com), which — cross-referenced with the classified Level_* corpus resident in OneDrive\Documents — demonstrates a second, concurrent cloud channel rather than a single path. The sent-byte direction is the load-bearing detail: it distinguishes genuine egress from the benign 551 MB received (client updates), so the conclusion rests on transmitted, not merely downloaded, volume.
scenes.what_it_means: The classified material did not just leave the building once — it left over two separate cloud channels under the insider's own accounts. The Dropbox leg is the strongest single proof of completed exfiltration in the case: the upload is timestamped in Dropbox's own database, corroborated by the operating system's tamper-independent network ledger, and the uploaded file is hash-matched to the recovered disguised archive. Because SRUM is an OS artifact the subject did not (and largely could not) sanitize, it survives the anti-forensic wipe that targeted the local Dropbox folder and cache, making the dual-channel egress conclusion robust. Honest scope limits: SRUM proves bytes were sent by these applications, and aggregation.dbx names the uploaded object and account — the precise file-by-file contents transmitted over OneDrive are inferred from the resident OneDrive\Documents corpus, not from a per-file transfer log, so the OneDrive leg is asserted as an active transmitting channel rather than a file-level upload manifest.

scenes.title: Anti-Forensic Destruction Defeated by Volume Shadow Copies
scenes.mitre: T1070.004 (Indicator Removal: File Deletion); related T1530
scenes.key_fact: The subject ran SysInternals SDelete to secure-wipe the original staged files (last of 10 executions at 2016-06-30 01:30:52 UTC), deleted the SDelete prefetch to erase proof of execution, and purged the 1.9 GB local Dropbox folder 2m12s after upload — but the 2016-10-14 and 2016-11-04 Volume Shadow Copies preserved the wiped 0-byte archive, the deleted prefetch, and the Dropbox cache, defeating the destruction entirely.

artifacts.source: Prefetch (live volume, Eric Zimmerman PECmd) + Amcache.hve
artifacts.locator: C:\Windows\Prefetch — SDELETE.EXE ×10, last run 2016-06-30 01:30:52 UTC; Amcache.hve sdelete.exe SHA1 ab48396a
artifacts.shows: SDelete actually executed 10 times, the final run at 01:30:52 — proving the secure-wipe of originals occurred (the act the deletion below tried to hide).

artifacts.locator: vss2_fls.txt deleted(*) entries: Windows/Prefetch/SDELETE.EXE-FBA93810.pf ; Users/defaultprinter/Desktop/temp.zip (0 bytes) ; $RECYCLE.BIN/S-1-5-21-3739107332-290452467-3466442662-1001/$RK7QVJQ/.dropbox.cache/… (284,067 B)
artifacts.shows: The shadow copy preserved the deleted SDelete prefetch, the SDelete-wiped temp.zip collapsed to 0 bytes, and the purged Dropbox cache — the exact items the subject tried to destroy, recovered intact.

artifacts.locator: C:\$Recycle.Bin — $I record for C:\Users\PC User\Dropbox, 1,908,571,018 bytes, deleted 2016-06-30 01:48:48 UTC
artifacts.shows: The 1.9 GB local Dropbox folder was deleted 2m12s after the 01:46:06 upload completed — coordinated post-exfil cleanup, not routine housekeeping.

scenes.correlation: The three artifacts come from independent stores and lock together temporally and logically. The live-volume Prefetch/Amcache prove SDelete RAN (10 executions, last 01:30:52) — but Prefetch on the live volume for that run was itself deleted; the VSS Store2 differential independently recovers the very file (SDELETE.EXE-FBA93810.pf) that was deleted to erase that proof, closing the loop: execution is proven even though the executor tried to remove its trace. The same VSS store recovers temp.zip as a 0-byte husk — the unmistakable signature of an SDelete overwrite (file metadata survives, content zeroed) — corroborating that the named staging archive was the wipe target. The Recycle Bin $I timestamp (01:48:48) sits exactly 2m12s after the Dropbox upload completion (01:46:06, established in Scene on cloud egress) and 18 minutes after the SDelete run, placing all three destruction acts in one tight, ordered post-exfiltration cleanup window. Because the 2016-10-14/11-04 snapshots were taken AFTER every deletion, the VSS copy is a point-in-time preservation that the subject could not reach — cross-source agreement (live Prefetch says it ran; VSS says here is what you deleted; $I says when and how big) makes the anti-forensic intent and its failure mutually corroborating.
scenes.what_it_means: This is the consciousness-of-guilt centerpiece: the subject did not merely take data, he deliberately tried to destroy the evidence of taking it — secure-wiping originals, deleting the prefetch that proved the wipe tool ran, and purging the cloud-client folder and cache minutes after the upload. None of it worked. Volume Shadow Copies, a Windows backup mechanism the subject did not account for, preserved a snapshot of exactly what he tried to erase, so the wiped archive, the deleted execution record, and the purged cache are all back in the examiner's hands. For a jury this both proves the anti-forensic acts and demonstrates intent, while the honest scope holds: this is file-deletion tradecraft defeated by VSS — no malware, no implant, and no claim beyond what the recovered artifacts show.

closing_fact: Taken together, the evidence proves a complete insider trade-secret theft executed end-to-end by one trusted principal, PC User / Anthony Vanko, using only valid credentials and legitimate signed software — no malware, no external breach, no implant. Eight scenes drawn from independent artifact classes (NTUSER and SOFTWARE registry hives, $MFT $SI timestamps, Security.evtx audit records, Recycle Bin $I/$R metadata, Prefetch/Amcache execution traces, the Dropbox aggregation.dbx catalog, the tamper-independent SRUM network ledger, a Gmail OST mailbox, and libvshadow Volume Shadow Copies) interlock on a single consistent timeline: collection by file-COPY from \\\\STARK-FILESERVE (2016-04-30 18:10) -> creation of the masquerade staging mule \"defaultprinter\" and a 2.6 MB classified archive on its Desktop (2016-06-18) -> active open of a Level-12 \"Project Nehemiah\" document raising realized exposure above the assumed tier -> two-way coordination with the foreign-recruiter channel (2016-06-27 21:22:49) -> 7-Zip disguise as \"vacation photos.7z\" (hash b210bcd8…, 2016-06-30 01:28) -> dual Dropbox+OneDrive cloud exfil (01:46:06) -> SDelete wipe and folder/prefetch purge (01:30:52 / 01:48:48). The same SHA-256 binds the recovered archive to the Dropbox upload record; the same VSS snapshots that defeated the wipe also preserved the Level-12 lock file and the wiped temp.zip. The conclusions are deliberately bounded to what the artifacts support — the three email attachments were never extracted (so no email-borne classified transfer is claimed), classified content is established by copy-provenance rather than content-scan, and the OneDrive leg is asserted as an active transmitting channel rather than a file-level manifest — and that honesty is what makes the proven chain unassailable.
outro_line: A textbook insider case where the strongest evidence is not what the subject did, but what he tried to erase — and could not.
